title: Impact of financial literacy, mental budgeting and self control on financial wellbeing: Mediating impact of investment decision making
tldr: Financial literacy, mental budgeting, and self-control significantly improve financial wellbeing, with investment decision-making partially mediating these relationships in a sample of 449 Chinese university students.
problem_and_motivation: Financial wellbeing is a growing concern in personal and household finance, with mental health issues like depression and anxiety linked to financial stress. While financial literacy, mental budgeting, and self-control are known to influence financial outcomes, their combined effects and the mediating role of investment decision-making remain underexplored. There is a need to understand how cognitive factors jointly influence subjective financial wellbeing, particularly among younger populations facing economic uncertainty from events like the Great Recession and COVID-19 pandemic.
approach: Survey data collected from 449 Chinese university students using convenience sampling through physical and electronic channels.
Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) used for path analysis and mediation testing.
Financial literacy measured using seven items adapted from previous studies, mental budgeting using four items from household finance management research.
Self-control measured using a shorter version of the Brief Self-Control Scale (five items) plus four items from the Short-Term Future Orientation Scale.
Investment decision-making behavior scale adopted with four components: overall financial management, savings and investment, cash management, and credit management.
Mediation analysis following Baron and Kenny approach to test simultaneous direct and indirect effects.
findings: num: Financial literacy has the strongest positive direct effect on financial wellbeing (β=0.299, p=0.000).
num: Self-control has the second strongest direct effect (β=0.182, p=0.000).
num: Mental budgeting has a positive direct effect (β=0.102, p=0.000).
num: Investment decision-making positively affects financial wellbeing (β=0.126, p=0.059).
num: Financial literacy → Investment decision-making path coefficient is 0.136 (p=0.000).
num: Mental budgeting → Investment decision-making path coefficient is 0.128 (p=0.000).
num: Self-control → Investment decision-making path coefficient is 0.152 (p=0.000).
num: Investment decision-making partially mediates all three relationships (indirect effects: 0.017, 0.016, 0.019 respectively, all p<0.05).

definitions.definition: Knowledge of basic financial concepts, ability to apply financial knowledge and skills in managing financial resources effectively, and ability to make informed financial decisions.
The cognitive process that people use to organize, evaluate, and keep track of financial activities, involving categorizing and monitoring expenses and income mentally.
The ability to control one's conduct and reduce impulsivity, enabling rational financial decision-making aligned with long-term goals.
A subjective evaluation of one's present and future financial situation, encompassing both financial anxiety and financial security dimensions.
The process of making decisions related to finances and investments, influenced by financial knowledge, attitude, behavior, self-control, and psychological biases.
Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling, a variance-based approach flexible with sample sizes and less vulnerable to violations of multivariate data assumptions.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study provides empirical evidence that financial literacy, mental budgeting, and self-control jointly influence subjective financial wellbeing, with investment decision-making partially mediating these relationships. The PLS-SEM analysis on 449 Chinese university students reveals that financial literacy has the strongest direct effect (β=0.299), followed by self-control (β=0.182) and mental budgeting (β=0.102). The partial mediation through investment decision-making suggests that cognitive and behavioral factors translate into financial outcomes partly through improved decision-making behavior. These findings support the development of financial tools that integrate budgeting support, literacy education, and self-control mechanisms.
directly_justifies: Financial literacy is the strongest predictor of financial wellbeing (β=0.299, p=0.000), supporting financial education initiatives.
Mental budgeting has a significant positive impact on financial wellbeing (β=0.102, p=0.000), validating budget-based financial tools.
Self-control significantly influences both investment decision-making and financial wellbeing, highlighting the importance of behavioral interventions.
Investment decision-making partially mediates all three relationships, suggesting that improved decision-making behavior channels cognitive skills into financial outcomes.
All measurement constructs achieve acceptable reliability (CR > 0.70) and validity (AVE > 0.50) thresholds.
limits: Convenience sampling of Chinese university students limits generalizability to broader and more diverse populations.
Cross-sectional design prevents establishing causal relationships between the variables.
Self-reported measures may introduce response biases and social desirability effects.
Investment decision-making path coefficient is marginally significant (p=0.059), weakening the mediation evidence.
No objective financial behavior measures were used to validate self-reported financial wellbeing.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. High relevance was assigned to budgeting strategies and methodologies (7.A) as mental budgeting is a primary construct. Medium relevance was assigned to budgeting systems and tools (7.B) because findings inform system design, and engagement dynamics (11.A) because self-control and mental budgeting relate to user engagement in financial systems. Topics rejected include Filipino-specific topics (1.A-1.C, 2.A-2.D), expense categorization (3.A-3.C), personal finance systems (4.A-4.B), classification approaches (5.A-5.C), predictive modeling (6.A-6.C), anomaly detection (8.A-8.B), mobile design (9.A-9.C), data privacy (10.A-10.B), evaluation frameworks (12.A-12.C), savings/debt management (13.A-13.C), and synthetic data generation (14.A). The paper examines behavioral and cognitive determinants of financial wellbeing rather than system design or algorithm development.

limitations: Convenience sampling of Chinese university students limits generalizability to broader and more diverse populations.
Cross-sectional design prevents establishing causal relationships between the variables.
Self-reported measures may introduce response biases and social desirability effects.
Investment decision-making path coefficient is marginally significant (p=0.059), weakening the mediation evidence.
No objective financial behavior measures were used to validate self-reported financial wellbeing.
remember_this: Financial literacy is the strongest predictor of financial wellbeing (β=0.299) among cognitive factors studied.
Mental budgeting and self-control both significantly improve financial wellbeing through direct and mediated pathways.
Investment decision-making partially mediates the relationship between all three predictors and financial wellbeing.
All constructs achieve acceptable psychometric properties (CR > 0.70, AVE > 0.50) with PLS-SEM.
Findings support integrating financial education, budgeting tools, and self-control mechanisms in personal finance systems.
